title: Lateness Index & Adaptive Batcher — Field Notes
summary: Notes from small-scale experiments that explore an operational metric we call 'lateness index' and its use to drive runtime batcher adaptivity. Practical checklist, run outputs, and hypotheses for follow-ups.
content:
Purpose:
- Try a lighter-weight signal to drive batching decisions that correlates with tail latency without needing full quantile tracing everywhere.
- Evaluate soft deadline vs hard timeout strategies when paired with lateness index-based demotion.
- Understand fairness implications when aggressive coalescing is applied to mixed-priority traffic.

Quick description of lateness index (LI):
- LI = (observed_flush_delay_ms / configured_soft_deadline_ms).
- intuition: when LI > 1, the request waited longer than its targeted deadline; we use per-slot LI estimates (EWMA).
- we experimented with class-specific EWMA windows (10s, 30s) to avoid overreacting to brief spikes.

Experiment matrix (grid):
- target_batch_size: [8, 16, 32]
- soft_deadline_ms: [12, 25, 50]
- hard_timeout_ms: [200, 500] (used as safety flush)
- fairness_weight: [0.1, 0.5, 1.0] (0.1 biases toward throughput, 1.0 strict fairness)
- LI_trigger_threshold: [0.8, 1.0, 1.2] (when to open a demotion lane)

Workloads used:
- steady-qps: 150 req/s, single-token median=6 tokens (small chat), tailiness low
- burst-qps: periodic 2s bursts to 800 req/s for 200ms window (simulates user spikes)
- mixed-priority: 70% low-prio (background), 30% high-prio (interactive) interleaved
- synthetic latency-fat clients: long-sequence requests to stress KV-cache interaction

Instrumentation & commands we ran (notes):
- tracing: enabled lightweight tracer (sample 1%) for fine-grained estimation; used trace id mapping in run logs.
- perf counters: linux perf top during heavy bursts to watch syscall backpressure.
- GPU profiling: nvidia-smi dmon + nvprof for kernel timeline on a subset of runs (helpful to see kernel batching efficiency).
- local flamegraphs: py-spy record --native -o flame.svg PID (for python host code); perf script -> FlameGraph for C++ runtime bits.
- scheduler debug: --emit-slot-metrics and --slot-ewma for 30s window per class.

Key observations (selected):
1) LI correlates well with P95/P99 only when EWMA window aligned to burst duration.
   - 10s EWMA captured brief spikes too noisily; 30s too sluggish for quick adaptation. 15s ended up being a good middle ground in follow-ups.
2) Soft-deadline (25ms) + LI-based demotion reduced tail amplification vs hard-timeout-only.
   - when LI>1.0, we opened a demotion lane that forced smaller batches for the affected priority class. This prevented long waits for other lanes.
3) Aggressive target_batch_size=32 + fairness_weight=0.1 gave best throughput but P99 regressed under burst.
4) Mixed-priority runs reveal starvation patterns: low fairness_weight causes high-prio to monopolize slot formation due to arrival clustering; fairness_weight>=0.5 mitigated but at throughput cost.
5) KV-cache churn interacts badly with large-batch coalescing for long-sequence clients — cache miss storms add 5-10ms jitter which LI picks up quickly.

Representative run excerpt (text log condensed):
- run id: li-experiment-aug12-16:42
- params: batch=16 soft_deadline=25 hard=500 fairness=0.5 LI_thresh=1.0 ewma=30s
- metrics: avg_lat_ms=18 P95=32 P99=58 qps=140 gpu_util=78%
- LI summary: classA_EWMA=0.62 classB_EWMA=1.12 -> demotion triggered for classB at 16:45:03
- action: opened demotion lane (max_batch=8) for classB, immediate P99 drop from 98->60 over 8s
- note: small transient throughput dip 3% during lane reconfiguration

Profiling notes (what was surprising):
- Kernel launch batching was efficient; major CPU time was in slot allocation and eviction bookkeeping when demotion lanes proliferated.
- Perf shows 20% time spent in futex/syscall path under heavy bursts — suggests contention on slot mutexes.
- When demotion lane count > 3, scheduling overhead rises nonlinearly. Keep demotion lanes limited; collapse demotion buckets by affinity rather than per-request.

Hypotheses and follow-ups:
- Hypothesis A: A two-tier EWMA (fast 5s + slow 30s) will let us react to short spikes while preserving stability. Test matrix suggested.
- Hypothesis B: Replace per-slot mutex with per-shard lock to reduce futex contention (microbenchmarking required).
- Hypothesis C: Add KV-cache-miss-aware inflight counter to avoid treating cache-induced jitter as scheduling failure.

Short checklist for next run (immediate actions):
- Add `--ewma-fast=5s --ewma-slow=30s` flags and expose combined LI metric.
- Implement demotion-lane cap (max 2) and affinity collapse heuristic.
- Run microbenchmark for lock sharding with synthetic contention (script attached in linked PR).
- Gather nvprof traces for runs where GPU_util < 60% despite high qps — looks like CPU-side stall.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is acceptable transient throughput loss when demoting? need product-level SLO guidance.
- Should LI be exported to Console as an early warning? dashboard sketch in Confluence, needs PM feedback.
- How to tune LI thresholds per-customer basis: safe defaults vs tuned profiles.

Notes to self:
- Logs vs traces: prefer traces for root-cause, logs for signal. Keep sampling light.
- Save candidate runs with trace coverage greater than 10% for later analysis.
- Add a small gamified chart to Console to show "lateness pressure" for debugging during incidents.

Attachments / artifacts (local):
- raw run CSVs: s3://redwood-run-bench/li-experiments/aug12-aug20/
- flamegraphs: li-aug12-flame.svg, li-aug14-cpu-flame.svg
- PR w/ scheduler flags: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-runtime/pull/4123

Decision: Continue with two-tier EWMA + demotion cap experiments. Prioritize lock-sharding microbenchmark next sprint.

If you take anything from this doc: start small (batch 16, soft 25ms, ewma fast=5 slow=30, demotion_cap=2) and iterate.

End of notes.
